name: libutf
baseline: ICU 78.3 (ICU4C: ubrk grapheme break iterator, unorm2 NFC, ucol DUCET collation)

Core-to-core with ICU on native UTF-16: NFC 28 ms vs 39 ms (1.4x faster), grapheme segmentation 237 ms vs 277 ms (1.2x faster), but DUCET collation 31 ms vs 22 ms (ICU 1.4x faster).

hardware: MacBook Pro, Apple M5 Max (stated in README)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (new repo, first visible commit 2026-03-24); code extracted from TinyMUX, in production there since 2008
tradeoffs: Pure C11, no malloc, no dependencies, 702 KB static library versus about 42 MB for ICU static libraries (README). Works directly on UTF-8 with compressed DFAs, so its advantage is largest when the application holds UTF-8 and ICU has to convert to UTF-16. Covers only grapheme segmentation, NFC, collation (DUCET), classification and case/width tables; no word, sentence or line-break segmentation, no bidi, no locale-tailored collation, no shaping. Unicode 16.0.
caveats: First-party benchmark on a tiny corpus of short hand-written strings repeated many times, so it measures per-call overhead more than bulk throughput. Times are totals for a fixed iteration count, not per-operation rates. The headline 1.3x to 3.8x numbers include ICU's UTF-8 to UTF-16 conversion; core-to-core the gaps shrink (1.2x and 1.4x) and ICU wins collation by 1.4x. ICU build configuration and compiler version are not stated. Category fit is marginal: this is Unicode text segmentation, normalization and collation, not font shaping or rasterization, so the named category baselines (HarfBuzz, FreeType) do not apply; the baseline is ICU, as for uni-algo. NFC and collation are differentially tested against ICU (README), the README lists a 499-test suite, but grapheme segmentation conformance was not checked here.

claimed_speedup: Snippet only: versus the x265 veryslow preset uavs3e gives average BD-rate savings of 22.7% (luma) and 46.1% / 46.2% (chroma); the uAVS3e RealTime encoder shows 'a significant advantage in encoding speed compared to x265' (no ratio seen) and is described as capable of real-time processing up to 8K.
stars_or_usage: 162 stars; Peking University Shenzhen Graduate School / Peng Cheng Laboratory
tradeoffs: Encodes AVS3-P2 baseline profile, not HEVC, so it is not a drop-in x265 replacement; SSE4/AVX2 and ARM paths; 10-bit support.
caveats: Snippet only: numbers come from search snippets of the IEEE paper 'An Efficient and Open Source Encoder Uavs3e for Video Compression' and a later real-time paper (blocked, not opened); the repo README has no numbers. The comparison crosses codecs (AVS3 vs HEVC). Licence is described as BSD 4-clause with custom copyright text, with an advertising clause. No speed ratio was seen.

name: VVenC
baseline: VTM-19.2 (JVET VVC reference encoder) and HM-17.0 (HEVC reference encoder); x265 v3.5 is also plotted but only in figures
workload: Random-access encoding of JVET common-test-condition HD and UHD sequences at QP 22/27/32/37, VVenC with 8 threads, reported as encoder runtime speedup together with PSNR BD-rate versus HM-17.0.
claimed_speedup: VVenC v1.14.0 Table III (HD4K): faster preset 2400x, fast 1100x, medium 330x, slow 87x, slower 19x faster than VTM-19.2 (HD column: 2400x/1100x/280x/74x/15x); versus HM-17.0 the same presets are 380x/180x/53x/14x/3x faster with PSNR BD-rate of -13.3%/-25.8%/-35.1%/-39.1%/-42.1%. Page text: slower preset reaches VTM-like BD-rate with more than 20x speedup over VTM. Speedups versus x265 are shown only as a figure (no numbers in text).
hardware: AMD EPYC 7502P 32-Core @2.5GHz (Dell servers); VVenC and x265 run with 8 threads, HM and VTM single-threaded
tradeoffs: Encodes H.266/VVC, whose decoder support and patent licensing differ from H.264/HEVC; the speedups are relative to the slow JVET reference software, not to a production encoder. Perceptual tuning (XPSNR-based QPA) is available.
caveats: First-party wiki numbers; compiler, flags and thread pinning not stated, so not reproducible-tier. The baselines in the numeric tables (VTM, HM) are research reference encoders and are single-threaded, so the headline multipliers (hundreds to thousands of x) say little about speed versus x265 or x264. The x265 v3.5 comparison (PSNR and MS-SSIM tuned, 8 threads) appears only as figures. Page cites peer-reviewed VVenC papers that were not opened (IEEE and ACM are blocked here).
